analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety enforcement, penalties, and miner rights, and extends OSHA protection to government workers.
analysis.headline: A mine and workplace safety bill with four Democratic cosponsors was referred to the Senate labor committee in April 2013 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill was written in response to the 2010 Upper Big Branch mine explosion that killed 29 miners, which investigations found was preventable. It would have required independent investigations of major mining accidents, given miners and their families a bigger role in inspections, raised fines for safety violations, held company officers personally liable, protected miners who refuse unsafe work, mandated safety equipment and training, and extended federal workplace safety law to state and local government employees for the first time. It was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners, families of miners killed or injured on the job, and — through the OSHA expansion — millions of state, county, and city government workers who currently have no federal workplace safety coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Miners, their families, and government employees

how_it_helps.text: Requires an independent accident investigation, with subpoena power, for any mine accident involving three or more deaths, in addition to the government's own investigation [S2][S3].

Lets miners speak privately with investigators without the operator or its lawyers present, gives miners' representatives the right to join accident investigations, and lets a killed miner's closest relative designate a representative [S2][S3].

Raises civil penalties, including up to $150,000 per significant violation and doubled penalties for repeat-offender mines, and raises criminal penalties to as much as $1,000,000 in fines and five years' imprisonment, with personal liability for directors, officers, and agents who knowingly authorize violations [S3].

Protects miners who refuse work they reasonably believe is dangerous, and pays miners full wages for the entire time they are idled by a safety withdrawal order, instead of only the rest of a shift [S2][S3].

Mandates atmospheric monitoring systems, proximity detectors on mining equipment, stronger rock dusting to prevent explosions, quarterly self-rescue training, and a public database of every mine's safety record [S2][S3].

Expands the Occupational Safety and Health Act to cover federal, state, and local government employees, who are currently outside its protection, and adds victim rights and higher penalties for serious, willful, or repeated violations [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would face higher fines, new equipment and monitoring requirements, more training, and personal legal liability for executives, plus government employers newly subject to OSHA.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and government employers

drawbacks.text: The costs fall on mine operators — fines up to $150,000 per violation, doubled penalties for troubled mines, mandated monitoring and proximity-detection equipment, and expanded training — which an honest supporter should acknowledge could burden smaller mining companies and add to coal production costs [S3].

Extending OSHA to government employees would create new compliance and enforcement obligations for state and local governments, which would have to fund inspections and corrective actions without a dedicated funding stream in the bill [S2].

The bill makes regulatory criteria for 'pattern of violations' determinations a matter of federal regulation rather than statute and limits courts' ability to second-guess the agency's plan decisions, which operators argued concentrates enforcement discretion in one agency [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and grave: the 2010 Upper Big Branch explosion killed 29 miners and five separate investigations concluded it was preventable and caused by the operator's failure to follow known safety standards [S3]. The bill's costs are compliance spending and higher fines for an industry whose product already carries severe human risk. The main design concerns are cost pressure on small operators and expanded agency discretion, not the core safety mandates. On balance the bill is strongly weighted toward worker protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote; the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. John Rockefeller IV of West Virginia introduced the bill on April 24, 2013, joined by three Democratic cosponsors, citing the Upper Big Branch disaster that killed 29 miners and five investigations finding it preventable [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction; that was the last action recorded [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in the bill's action history through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off: no higher fines, no personal executive liability, no new equipment mandates, and no expanded miner rights ever took effect. Miners and the families of disaster victims gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal mine operators avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters, including the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican senator cosponsored the bill [S4], and it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have raised their fines as much as fourfold for serious violations, doubled penalties for pattern-of-violations mines, exposed executives to personal fines and prison terms, and required new equipment and training. Operators' interest in lower enforcement costs ran directly against the safety protections the bill offered miners.
Extending OSHA to public employees would have given government workers federal safety protection for the first time but imposed new inspection and compliance duties on their government employers.

The bill would have mandated atmospheric monitoring systems on all underground mines and proximity detectors on mobile mining equipment, creating demand for safety technology whose purpose is preventing explosions and deaths.

Independent contractors performing services at mines would have been brought under the definition of 'operator,' subjecting them to the same safety duties and penalties as mine owners, while their workers gained the bill's protections.
